transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hi, doctor. Thank you. Um... it's a little hard to explain exactly, but I guess what really made me finally pick up the phone and come in today is... well, you know, I'm an executive secretary, right? So my whole life, my entire career, is built around being proactive and highly organized. I'm usually the guy who is ten steps ahead of everyone else. 

But lately, the things that usually make me feel like myself... they just don't. Like, I usually do these long photography walks on the weekends, going down by the river with my camera, just waiting for the perfect morning light. And I mentor some kids at the local community center on Tuesday afternoons, which I've done for years. Honestly, even just the simple act of keeping a really clean, color-coded calendar—which usually gives me a lot of personal satisfaction—all of it has just started feeling incredibly flat. And heavy. Like, physically heavy to even think about doing. 

I just stopped initiating them entirely. I look at my camera sitting there on the shelf and I just... I don't feel the spark to pick it up. I don't email the volunteer coordinator to set up my hours. I just kind of sit there. It’s like the starter motor in my brain just gave out, you know? It's not even that I'm actively upset about it, it's just this heavy, blank flatness where my drive used to be, and it's starting to really bother me because I'm just not doing the things that make up my life anymore.
Do you still enjoy things that you used to find pleasurable, or has the pleasure gone away as well?

That is... well, that's a really interesting question, actually. Because, you see, I've spent a lot of time thinking about that exact distinction while I'm just sitting there in my living room. I mean, my apartment has this big bay window, right? It looks out over the street, and sometimes I just sit in this oversized armchair I got a few years ago—really comfortable chair, by the way, I always tell people in the office to invest in good lumbar support—and I'll just sit there and wonder, 'If I actually got up and went down to the river with my camera right now, would I even like it?' 

And honestly, doctor, I really don't know. I'm just not sure. Because I haven't actually forced myself to do any of it to find out. It's like... well, if you don't eat the cake, you don't know if it still tastes good, right? I just haven't had the energy to take that first bite. So I can't really say for sure if the actual enjoyment is gone, because I haven't been doing the things to test it. I mean, maybe if someone physically dragged me out to the community center and put me in front of the kids, maybe I'd smile and feel that old warmth? I don't know. But since I'm just not initiating anything, I really haven't noticed if the pleasure itself is gone, or just... just hibernating, I guess. I really go back and forth on it, to be honest with you. It's a tough thing to measure when you're just sitting still.
Do you feel sad most of the time?

Sad? Hmm... you know, that's another one of those words that feels a bit tricky right now. Sad. Like, when I think of being sad, I think of crying, or feeling this deep, aching sorrow, you know? Like when my golden retriever, Buster, passed away about five years ago. That was sadness. I cried for days, I couldn't look at his leash hanging by the door. But this? What I'm feeling now? It's... it's not really like that. 

I wouldn't say I feel sad most of the time. It's more like... well, like I was saying before about the flatness. It's just this heavy, gray neutral. I don't feel like crying. I don't feel heartbroken or anything. I just feel... blank. Like the volume on my emotions has been turned all the way down to zero. So, no, I don't think 'sad' is the right word for it at all. It's just this really profound lack of feeling much of anything, which, in a way, is almost stranger than being sad, don't you think? Because at least when you're sad, you know you're feeling something. You're reacting to something. But this is just... nothing. Just a whole lot of nothing taking up space where my feelings used to be.
How long have you been feeling this way?

Well, let's see... time is such a funny thing to track when every day feels exactly like the last, isn't it? But if I really sit down and trace it back... I'd say it's been about a year and three months. Give or take a couple of weeks. 

I remember it pretty specifically because it all started around this very particular shift in my family dynamic. You see, a family member of mine—well, their health took a pretty significant turn. And it wasn't just their physical health, it was their behavior, too. Everything just kind of shifted, and suddenly there was this massive vacuum of responsibility that needed filling. And, well, like I told you, I'm an executive secretary. I coordinate things for a living. I organize, I schedule, I manage crises before they even happen. So, naturally, I stepped up and took on all that extra coordination for them. 

I was making the phone calls, setting up the appointments, managing the paperwork—all the things you do when someone you care about can't do it themselves. And at first, I just thought I was tired. You know, just standard, run-of-the-mill exhaustion from burning the candle at both ends. I figured anyone would be tired doing all that on top of a full-time job. But then the acute crisis part kind of settled down, the routines were in place, and I thought, 'Okay, now I can breathe. Now I can go back to my photography and the community center.' 

But... I didn't. The exhaustion never lifted, it just sort of morphed into this heavy, blank feeling I was telling you about. So, yeah, it's been about fifteen months now of just... sitting in that armchair, looking at my camera, and feeling absolutely nothing about it. It's really quite frustrating when you think about how long it's been going on. You'd think a person would just snap out of it eventually, right? But here I am, a year and three months later, still just... stuck in neutral.
Do you think you would enjoy activities like photography or mentoring if you were actually doing them, or do you think the pleasure from those activities is truly gone?

Well, see, that's exactly the crux of it. That's the whole reason I finally made the appointment to come in and talk to someone. Because... well, I don't know if the pleasure is truly gone forever, like it's been erased from my brain, or if it's just buried under all this... this heaviness. 

But what really scared me, what made me realize I couldn't just keep waiting it out in my armchair, is that the things that usually make me feel like *me*—you know, my photography walks down by the river where I try to catch the light just right on the water, or mentoring the kids at the community center, which I used to look forward to all week, or even just the simple satisfaction of keeping a perfectly clean, color-coded calendar at work... all of that just started feeling so incredibly flat. And heavy. Like every single thing, even the good things, weighed a hundred pounds. 

And because it felt so heavy, I just... I stopped initiating any of it. I stopped picking up the camera. I stopped volunteering. I didn't even care if my calendar was a mess, which, for an executive secretary, is practically a cardinal sin. So to answer your question, I don't know if I'd enjoy them if I forced myself to do them right now, but the fact that I can't even bring myself to try, that this flatness has just completely taken over... that's what brought me here today. It's just not like me to drop everything I care about like this.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past year?

Weight changes? Well... let me think about that for a second. 

You know, working in an executive office, I have a very specific rotation of clothes. Slacks, mostly. I actually get them tailored at this little place downtown because I like a very crisp, professional fit. When you're managing the front office for the executives, you have to look put together, and if you gain even a few pounds, or lose them, you feel it immediately in a tailored waistband, you know? It either pinches when you sit down at your desk, or it sags and you have to pull your belt a notch tighter. 

But... no, I haven't noticed anything like that. My clothes fit exactly the same as they did before all this started. 

It's actually a bit surprising, to be perfectly honest with you. Because with everything I was just telling you about—that heaviness, just sitting in the armchair staring at the wall—my routine is completely shot. I used to be so meticulous about my meals. I'd spend Sunday afternoons doing all this prep work, roasting vegetables, portioning out these little containers for the office fridge so I wouldn't be tempted by whatever pastries someone brought into the breakroom. I had a whole system. Now? Now I just... I grab whatever's easiest. A frozen dinner, a piece of toast, maybe a bowl of cereal. I just don't have the drive to stand there and chop vegetables anymore. It feels like too much work. But I guess, despite all that, I must be taking in roughly the same amount of food, because my weight hasn't fluctuated at all. It's just stayed completely steady through this whole fifteen months. So, no, no significant changes there.
Have you noticed any changes in your desire to be around friends or family?

Well, it's funny you ask that, because it ties right back into what I was trying to explain earlier about why I finally decided to make this appointment. You know, I was talking about the photography walks and the mentoring... and I guess it's all part of the same big picture. 

Before all this started, I was very social. I mean, you kind of have to be in my line of work, right? As an executive secretary, you're the gatekeeper. You're greeting people, making small talk with the board members, remembering whose daughter just started college and whose dog had surgery. And I was good at it! I enjoyed it. And outside of work, too. I'd go to the community center, I'd see my family, I'd meet up with friends from my old camera club. 

But lately... over this past year and a bit... it's just like I was saying before. Everything just feels so flat. And heavy. It's not just the hobbies, it's the people, too. It's like the energy it takes to pick up the phone and call a friend, or to agree to go over to my sister's house for dinner... it just feels insurmountable. I look at my phone when it rings, and I see a friend's name, and instead of feeling happy they're calling, I just feel this weight. Like, 'Oh no, I have to perform now. I have to sound interested. I have to find the energy to have a conversation.' 

And so I just don't. I let it go to voicemail. I make excuses. I tell them I'm busy with work, or that I'm just too tired from managing things for my family member, even though the acute part of that crisis is over. It's exactly like how I stopped initiating the photography or the mentoring. I just stopped initiating contact with people. I don't reach out. I don't make plans. I just sit in that armchair. 

And it's really distressing, honestly, because I know it's not me. I know I used to be the person who remembered everyone's birthday and organized the office happy hours. And now the thought of being in a room full of people, or even just sitting across from one friend at a coffee shop, just feels so exhausting that I can't even bring myself to try. So, yes, there's been a massive change there. I just... I don't have the drive to be around anyone anymore. It's all just part of that same heavy, flat feeling that made me come in here in the first place.
Do you often feel guilty about anything?

Guilty? No, not really. I mean, I guess you could say I feel bad about letting things slide, like I was saying with the calendar at work or not calling my friends back. It's not a great feeling to know you're not pulling your weight or being the friend you used to be. But it's not like a deep, consuming guilt, if that makes sense? 

It's more just... frustration. Frustration that I can't seem to muster the energy to do the things I know I should be doing. Like, I'll look at the dust gathering on my camera lenses on the shelf—I have a whole setup, you know, a 50mm prime lens, a nice telephoto, all neatly arranged—and I'll think, 'I really should take those out and clean them, or better yet, actually use them.' And I feel a little twinge of, I don't know, disappointment in myself? But it doesn't spiral into this huge guilt trip where I'm beating myself up over it for days. 

It's the same with work. When I misfiled that report last week—which, again, is just so unlike me, I'm usually the one catching other people's filing errors—I felt annoyed with myself. I thought, 'Come on, get it together.' But I didn't go home and agonize over it or feel like I was a terrible person or anything like that. It's just this pervasive sense that I'm not functioning at my normal capacity, and that's bothersome, certainly. But actual, heavy guilt? Like feeling worthless or like I've committed some awful sin? No, I haven't really been experiencing anything like that. It's mostly just that flatness I keep coming back to. It's hard to feel strongly enough about anything to even feel properly guilty about it, to be perfectly honest.
Have you ever thought about ending your life during this period of feeling flat and heavy?

Ending my life? Oh... no. No, definitely not. 

I know people probably assume that when you're just sitting in a chair all weekend staring at the wall, you must be in this dark, terrible, agonizing place where you just want it all to end. But it's really not like that for me. Like I was trying to explain, it's just... flat. It's a total lack of momentum. To actually think about ending my life... well, honestly, that feels like it would require a level of energy and, I don't know, active despair? And I just don't have that. I don't have the energy for a strong feeling like that. 

I mean, I've always been a very practical person. You absolutely have to be in my job. When you're managing the schedules and the daily crises of executive board members, you're constantly problem-solving and keeping things grounded. And even though I'm clearly not functioning at my best right now, and I'm letting things slide like that filing error I mentioned, my brain just doesn't go to that extreme. I don't sit in my living room thinking, 'I want to die.' I just sit there thinking... well, nothing, really. Or maybe just, 'I wish I had the energy to get up and make a proper cup of coffee instead of just drinking a glass of tap water.' 

It's almost like someone just unplugged me from the wall. I'm powered down. So, no, I haven't had any thoughts of suicide or hurting myself or anything of that nature. I don't want to die, I just... I'm just having a really, really hard time actively living my normal life right now, if you see the distinction. The thought of actually taking steps to end it all has never crossed my mind during these past fifteen months. It's just this heavy waiting. Just sitting there, waiting to feel like the guy who used to organize the office parties again.
Have you noticed yourself moving or speaking more slowly than you used to?

Moving or speaking slowly? Well, no, I wouldn't really say that. It is an interesting question, though, because you would think that with all this heaviness I keep talking about, I would be dragging myself around like a zombie. But it is not really like that. It is more about the motivation to move rather than the actual speed of the movement itself, if that makes sense. 

Like, at work, as an executive secretary, you have a very specific cadence you have to maintain. You absolutely cannot be dragging your words out when you have three different board members on hold and the vice president is asking for the quarterly projections. Just this past Tuesday, for instance, we had this massive scheduling conflict with the marketing team, and I had to coordinate between four different departments in the span of about twenty minutes. And I did it. I spoke at my normal, brisk pace, handled the calls, directed the traffic, so to speak. My voice did not sound sluggish, and I certainly was not moving in slow motion. 

Even walking in from the parking garage—which is a good quarter-mile walk, by the way, because they are doing construction on the east lot and the employee parking situation is just a complete nightmare right now—I am still walking at my usual clip. I am not shuffling my feet or taking forever to get from point A to point B. 

So, no, the actual physical speed of my arms and legs, or how fast the words come out of my mouth, that has not changed at all. I still sound exactly like me. It is just... like I said before, it is the initiation of the movement that is the hurdle. Once I am up and walking to the copier, I am moving fine. It is just getting out of that armchair in the first place. But once I am in motion, or once I actually start a conversation, my speed is completely normal. I just have fewer conversations these days.
Do you think you would still enjoy activities like photography or mentoring if you actually participated in them?

That is the million-dollar question, isn't it? Because I actually tried to test that out. A while back, I forced myself to take my camera—the one with the 50mm prime lens I was telling you about earlier—down to the botanical gardens. I've been going there for years because the morning light hitting the dew on the ferns is usually just spectacular. It's the kind of thing that usually completely centers me. But when I got there, and I was looking through the viewfinder... it was just... nothing. It didn't give me that spark at all. 

Honestly, doctor, that is exactly what made me come in to see you in the first place. The realization that the things that usually make me feel like myself—like those photography walks, or mentoring the kids, or even just keeping a perfectly clean, color-coded calendar at work—they all just started feeling incredibly flat and heavy. 

Take the mentoring, for example. I work with this group of high school sophomores at the community center, helping them with college prep and organizational skills. As an executive secretary, organizing is my bread and butter, and usually, seeing a kid finally figure out how to manage their study schedule gives me a real boost. It makes me feel like I'm contributing, like I'm myself. But the last few times I went, I was sitting there in the folding chair, looking at these kids I genuinely care about, and the whole experience was just... heavy. There was no joy in it. It felt like a chore. 

Because everything started feeling so flat and heavy, I just stopped initiating them. I stopped waking up early for the photo walks, I told the community center coordinator I needed to take a step back from the kids for a while, and, as I mentioned, I let the calendar slide at the office. I just stopped doing the things that make me, well, me. And that was a real wake-up call. It's one thing to feel tired or unmotivated to do the dishes, but when you completely lose the connection to your own passions and the things that define your life... well, I realized I couldn't just keep sitting in my armchair waiting for it to pass. I needed to figure out why everything I love suddenly feels like a hundred-pound weight, which is why I finally made this appointment.
Do you think you've lost interest in the activities you used to enjoy?

Yeah, exactly. I mean, that's really the crux of it, like I was just saying. That realization is exactly what made me come in to see you. It's this total loss of interest where the things that usually make me feel like myself—you know, the photography walks I mentioned, mentoring those high school kids, or even just the simple satisfaction of keeping a perfectly clean, color-coded calendar at the office—they all just started feeling so completely flat and heavy. 

It's like someone turned down the volume on my entire personality. "Losing interest" almost sounds too mild, honestly. It's more like the drive just evaporated. Because I don't have that interest or that spark anymore, I just stopped initiating them entirely. 

I used to be the guy who was always planning the next photo shoot, checking the weather apps the night before for the best morning lighting, making sure my lenses were packed. Or I'd be the one emailing the community center coordinator on a Tuesday with new college prep materials for the kids to use on Thursday. I was always starting things, always looking ahead. But lately? I look at my camera bag sitting by the front door, or I think about calling the youth center, and it just feels like trying to push a boulder up a hill. It's just this immense heaviness. So I just don't do it. I don't start anything. 

I just sit in my chair instead. And when you stop initiating all the things that actually make up your life, the things that give you your identity... well, you realize you're not really living it anymore. You're just existing. Which, again, is why I'm sitting here in your office. It's just so incredibly frustrating to know what I *should* want to do, and to remember how much I used to love those things, but to have absolutely zero drive to actually go do them.
Do you find yourself having difficulty getting out of bed in the morning?

Getting out of bed? Well, no, not exactly. I mean, I don't just lie there staring at the ceiling for hours on end, unable to throw the covers off. It's not like that. I still get up. I have to get up, right? I have an alarm set for 6:15 AM every weekday, and usually a backup set for 6:25 AM, just in case, though I rarely need the backup. 

My morning routine is pretty established. I get up, I make my coffee—usually a dark roast, French press, because I find the drip machines just don't extract the oils properly, you know? And I need that strong cup of coffee to even start thinking about facing the day, especially with the commute I have. I live out in the suburbs, so if I don't leave by exactly 7:35, I hit the school traffic on Route 9, and then it's just a complete crawl all the way to the office park. 

So, physically getting out of the bed isn't the issue. I swing my legs over the side, I put my slippers on, and I start moving. It's more... well, it goes back to what I was saying about that heaviness. I get up, but I'm just going through the motions. I'm operating on pure routine and obligation. I know I have to be at my desk, logged into the system, and checking the VP's calendar before 8:30 AM, so I just do it. But the whole time I'm getting dressed, making the coffee, packing my lunch—which I've been doing less of lately, honestly, I've just been buying those overpriced salads from the cafeteria downstairs because making a sandwich just feels like too much effort—the whole time, I'm just feeling that flat, heavy sensation. 

I'm not lying in bed paralyzed, if that's what you mean. I'm up. I'm moving. But I'm not... I'm not waking up with any sort of energy or purpose, you know? I'm just getting out of bed because the alarm went off and I have a mortgage to pay. But the actual act of standing up and leaving the mattress? No, I don't have difficulty with that specific mechanical action. I just do it because I have to.
Do you feel like you're moving more slowly than you used to when you're doing everyday activities?

Moving more slowly? Um, no, I don't... I don't think so. I haven't really noticed anything like that, physically speaking. 

I mean, as an executive secretary, my entire day is dictated by pace, right? You have to be quick. I still type at about 85 words per minute, which is exactly where I've been for the last ten years. And when I'm walking around the office—our suite is on the fourth floor, and the main supply room with the heavy-duty copiers and the binding machines is all the way at the opposite end of the building, past the elevators and the breakroom—I'm still doing that walk at my normal, brisk pace. I have to. Mr. Henderson, the VP I support, he's one of those guys who expects things done yesterday. If I actually started physically moving slower, shuffling down the halls or taking twice as long to file the quarterly reports, he would absolutely notice and say something. 

So the mechanics of my movements, the actual physical speed of my arms and legs, that hasn't changed. It's just like what I was saying about getting out of bed. My body knows the routine and it executes the routine at the normal speed. Even at home, when I'm making that French press coffee I mentioned, my hands are doing the exact same motions at the exact same speed. I'm boiling the water, waiting exactly thirty seconds off the boil so I don't scorch the grounds, pouring, stirring... the physical timing is identical to how it was six months ago. 

It's really important to draw that distinction, I think. The *feeling* of doing these things is heavy, yes. Emotionally, mentally, it feels like a massive chore just to walk to the copier or plunge the coffee. But if you were watching me on a security camera or something, you wouldn't see a guy moving in slow motion. You'd just see a guy walking down a hallway at a perfectly normal speed. Honestly, if anything, there are times I probably try to rush through the physical tasks just to get them over with faster, just so I can get back to my desk or get back to my armchair at home and just... stop. So, no, I'm not moving any slower than I used to. It's just the internal drive that's stalled out, not my actual physical gears, if that makes sense.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight over the past year?

Weight loss? No, um, no, I haven't noticed anything like that. I mean, my clothes all still fit exactly the same. I wear these wool-blend trousers to the office—I always get the classic fit from Macy's because, let's face it, the slim fit just isn't practical or comfortable when you're sitting at a desk typing for eight or nine hours a day—and the waistband on those is exactly as snug as it was this time last year. 

I actually have a digital scale in my master bathroom, one of those smart ones that's supposed to sync to an app on your phone via Bluetooth. I haven't actually opened or synced the app in months because, well, like I was saying earlier about the effort, it just feels like one more unnecessary step to worry about. But I do still step on the scale itself every Tuesday morning. It's just baked into my Tuesday routine, right after I get out of the shower and before I put my undershirt on. And the numbers have been holding completely steady. I usually hover right around 185, maybe 186 if I had a heavier dinner on Monday night or if I'm retaining a little water. 

So, no, no significant weight loss. I mean, what do doctors even consider significant, anyway? Ten pounds? Twenty? Because my weight has been remarkably stable, really since my late twenties. I've just always stayed in that exact same zone. Even with this whole... this heavy feeling I was describing, and not wanting to make my own lunches anymore, my actual physical need to eat hasn't just disappeared. Like I said, I'm still going down to the building cafeteria at exactly 12:15 every day and buying those salads. If anything, I might have even gained a pound or two from whatever heavy dressing they pour on those things, because you know they don't use the light vinaigrette unless you specifically ask for it, and lately I just haven't had the energy to be that particular with the cashier. But no, to answer your question, my weight hasn't dropped at all. I'm exactly the same size I've been for years.
Do you wish you had more social interactions in your life?

More social interactions? I mean... it's complicated. It's not that I'm sitting at home lonely, pining for an invitation to a dinner party, you know? But... well, actually, this gets right to the heart of why I made the appointment to see you in the first place. 

I used to be pretty involved. I had these things that really made me feel like *me*, things that kept me connected to the world outside of the office. For example, I used to do these weekend photography walks. I have a Nikon D7500, which is a really solid mid-range DSLR, and I'd go downtown or out to the state park. Sometimes I'd go with a local meetup group, or sometimes I'd just walk around the Sunday farmer's market, interacting with the vendors and the crowds to get good candid street shots. And I was also mentoring kids—middle schoolers, mostly, through this community outreach program that my company sponsors. It was highly social, and really fulfilling, you know? Sitting down with them, helping them with their homework, talking to them about their futures. I was always the one organizing things, keeping a perfectly clean, color-coded personal calendar for all my extracurriculars and social obligations. I really prided myself on that level of engagement and organization. 

But lately... wishing for more social interaction implies that I actively have the drive for it right now. And that's just it—I don't. All of those things, the photography walks, mentoring the kids, even just the simple satisfaction of maintaining that clean calendar... it all just started feeling so incredibly flat. And heavy. There's that word again, heavy. It's like the color just drained out of the activities that used to define me. 

I didn't consciously decide to isolate myself, I just... I stopped initiating them. I stopped signing up for the weekend walks, I told the mentoring program coordinator I needed to take a step back, and I've let my personal calendar go completely blank outside of my work hours. And it's not that I'm sitting around wishing people would call me, it's that I wish I still *cared* enough to make the calls myself, if that makes sense. That's really what made me come in to see you. The fact that the things that usually make me feel like myself just feel like lifting a hundred-pound weight now, and I just can't bring myself to initiate any of it anymore.
Do you feel like you no longer enjoy activities that you used to find pleasurable?

Yeah, exactly. That's... that's really what I was just getting at a second ago. It's exactly that. The pleasure is just... gone. Like I was saying, that's the whole reason I made this appointment and came in to see you today. The things that usually make me feel like *me*—the photography walks with my Nikon, mentoring those middle schoolers on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons, even just the simple, everyday satisfaction of keeping a perfectly clean, color-coded calendar for all my events... it all just started feeling so incredibly flat. And heavy. 

It's like someone just turned down the volume on my ability to actually enjoy anything. I used to get such a thrill out of those activities, you know? Like, if I caught the perfect natural lighting on a Sunday morning at the farmer's market, or if one of the kids I mentor finally understood a difficult pre-algebra concept after we'd been working on it for an hour, I'd feel this rush of accomplishment. I'd come home and feel completely energized by it. It gave my weeks a real sense of purpose outside of the office. 

But now? If I even think about getting the camera out of its padded bag, or looking at my schedule to block out volunteer time, it just feels like a massive chore. There's no spark. No joy in it at all. It just feels entirely flat. So I just... I stopped initiating them. I stopped doing them entirely, because what's the point of forcing yourself through a hobby or a volunteer gig if the part of your brain that's supposed to actually enjoy it is just completely offline? It's incredibly frustrating because I know I *should* enjoy these things, I have a decade of memories proving that I love them, but the actual feeling of pleasure just isn't there anymore. So, yes, to answer your question, I definitely don't enjoy the things I used to.
Do you feel like you have enough energy to do the things you need to do?

Energy? Well... physical energy, yes. I mean, I'm not falling asleep at my desk or dragging my feet or anything like that. If we're talking about the actual physical battery power required to get through the day and do the mandatory things, I have plenty of it. 

I'm an executive assistant, and my job requires me to be completely "on" from the moment I walk into the building at 8:15 AM. I support two different senior vice presidents, which means I'm constantly managing their overlapping schedules, coordinating international travel across multiple time zones, and making sure all the briefing materials for the weekly steering committees are printed, perfectly bound, and distributed on time. You really can't do a job like that if you're physically exhausted. And I haven't missed a single day of work this entire year. 

I still get up at 6:00 AM every single morning without fail. The alarm goes off, I get out of bed, I take my shower, and I make my coffee. I always use a French press, usually a medium roast from this little local place a few blocks from my apartment, because I find that standard drip machines just make the beans taste incredibly burnt and bitter. Then I'm out the door and on the 7:10 train. I don't feel physically tired during any of this. My muscles don't ache, I'm not yawning all morning, and I'm certainly not trying to sneak naps in the breakroom in the middle of the afternoon. Just last Wednesday, I actually spent three hours standing up and completely reorganizing the physical filing cabinets in the main conference room just because the labeling system was getting a little sloppy. 

So, the energy to do what I *need* to do? The obligations? Yes, absolutely. I'm functioning perfectly fine on that front. The bills are paid on time, my wool trousers are dry-cleaned, my bosses are happy. It goes back to what I was trying to explain earlier—it's not a lack of physical energy or fatigue. It's just that heavy, flat feeling when it comes to the things outside of my obligations. The things I used to do just for myself.
